subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals because:
options: A high proportion of immune people reduces the chance of an unvaccinated person meeting an infected person
Antibodies are passed between people on contact
The pathogen mutates to become harmless
Vaccines spread immunity through the air
questions.explain: When enough of the population is immune, transmission is interrupted, so susceptible individuals are unlikely to encounter the pathogen.

questions.q: The clonal selection and activation of a specific B-cell typically requires:
options: Only the antigen binding to the B-cell receptor
Phagocytosis of the B-cell
Antigen binding plus stimulation by an activated T-helper cell releasing cytokines
Binding to a memory cell
questions.explain: Most B-cells require both antigen binding and signals (cytokines) from T-helper cells to divide and differentiate.

questions.q: An antigen is best defined as:
options: A toxin released by bacteria
An antibody produced by plasma cells
A protein that always causes disease
A molecule (usually protein) that is recognised as foreign and triggers an immune response
questions.explain: Antigens are molecules, often surface proteins, identified as non-self and capable of stimulating an immune response.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They destroy all the host's T-cells
They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: The secondary immune response is faster and stronger than the primary because:
options: Memory cells rapidly divide and differentiate into plasma cells, producing antibodies quickly
Phagocytosis no longer occurs
Antigens are weaker on second exposure
The pathogen has fewer antigens
questions.explain: Memory cells formed during the primary response allow a rapid proliferation of plasma cells and a higher, quicker antibody output.

questions.q: Antibodies passed from mother to baby in breast milk give the baby:
options: Artificial passive immunity
Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial active immunity
questions.explain: The antibodies are received naturally (via milk/placenta) and the baby does not make them itself, so it is natural passive immunity.

questions.q: During phagocytosis of a pathogen, the engulfed microbe is destroyed when:
options: The phagocyte divides by mitosis
Memory cells are produced directly
Antibodies are released into the cytoplasm
A phagosome fuses with a lysosome and lysozymes hydrolyse the pathogen
questions.explain: The pathogen is enclosed in a phagosome which fuses with a lysosome; lytic enzymes (lysozymes) then digest it.

questions.q: An antibody molecule's specificity for a particular antigen is determined by:
options: The disulfide bridges holding the chains together
The variable region, which forms the antigen-binding site
The hinge region between the chains
The constant region of the heavy chains
questions.explain: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains form a binding site whose shape is complementary to a specific antigen.

questions.q: In a pregnancy test, monoclonal antibodies are used to:
options: Produce hCG in the urine
Destroy the hCG hormone
Convert hCG into a dye
Bind specifically to the hCG hormone, giving a coloured line when present
questions.explain: Mobile antibodies bind hCG and are then trapped by immobilised antibodies in the test window, producing a visible coloured line.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as HIV?
options: Viruses lack the metabolic processes and structures (e.g. cell walls, ribosomes) that antibiotics target
Viruses have thicker cell walls
Viruses are too large to be affected
Antibiotics only work on fungi
questions.explain: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes; viruses use host-cell machinery and lack these targets, so antibiotics do not affect them.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies are described as 'monoclonal' because they are:
options: A mixture of antibodies against several antigens
Produced by many different B-cells
Made only inside the human body
Identical antibodies produced from a single clone of cells, all specific to one antigen
questions.explain: They are derived from one B-cell clone, so every antibody is identical and binds the same specific antigen.

questions.q: Plasma cells differ from memory cells in that plasma cells:
options: Secrete large quantities of antibody but are short-lived
Present antigens to T-cells
Remain in the blood for years
Divide rapidly on a second exposure
questions.explain: Plasma cells are antibody factories that live only a few days, whereas memory cells persist to give rapid future responses.
